attacks.claim: The purge commits the local DB deletion in one transaction and only then calls Amplitude, Customer.io, Zendesk, Stripe and Apple. A crash or failed call after commit removes the local record of what each processor still holds, so processor-side data can be orphaned with no durable record of what is owed; the purge-failed ticket is the only trace.
attacks.evidence: "each account is one DB transaction across `users` and the 23 tables that reference it." / "After the DB transaction commits:"

attacks.claim: Registry actions (delete vs nullify for rows owned by others) are irreversible and run nightly. The only verification is a dry-run on the first batch and a CI presence check, so a wrong action would silently delete other users' data in every later run. The purge job also ignores the feature flag and no kill switch or pause for it is described.
attacks.evidence: "lists every table with a `user_id` or `*_user_id` column and its action (delete, or nullify for rows owned by someone else)." / "Requests already confirmed are still purged on schedule (the purge job ignores the flag)"

attacks.claim: Art. 17 timing depends on a single manual privacy-lead gate for the first live batch, with no backup owner, SLA or stop condition. Processor failures open tickets with no resolution deadline, so erasure is not guaranteed within one month.
attacks.evidence: "the privacy lead checks the account list and per-table row counts before it runs live." / "anything still failing opens a `purge-failed` ticket for the privacy lead."

attacks.claim: Application logs and Sentry reports are not in the purge flow. Retention of 30 days means data created before a purge persists past the purge date, and the plan never states that this is covered by erasure.
attacks.evidence: "Application logs and Sentry error reports have 30-day retention (privacy policy §7)."

attacks.claim: The processor list omits systems that hold user-level data: the transactional email sender (which holds addresses and message content), push providers holding device tokens, and Google sign-in (only Apple is revoked). The claim that no other system holds user data rests on an inventory the plan does not show.
attacks.evidence: "No other system holds user-level data beyond the processors below (data inventory DPI-2026, reviewed Sep 2026)."

attacks.claim: Backups keep personal data for 35 days and are not edited, and the plan gives no erasure path for backup copies beyond the restore runbook. Backups are not cited in the privacy-policy disclosure the plan relies on.
attacks.evidence: "Postgres snapshots roll off after 35 days and are not edited." / "disclosed in privacy policy §7" (cited only for invoices)

attacks.claim: The registry CI test only detects columns named user_id or *_user_id. Tables referencing users through owner_id, sender_id or polymorphic subject columns are not caught, so erasure can silently miss data despite the claim that new tables cannot be forgotten.
attacks.evidence: "A CI test fails if any such column in `db/schema.rb` is missing from the registry, so new tables cannot be forgotten."

attacks.claim: App Store and Google Play subscriptions are not cancelled by the plan. The purge deletes the account while the store subscription keeps renewing, and the plan has no check that renewals stopped.
attacks.evidence: "Deleting your account does not cancel your App Store subscription" / "we cannot cancel these."

attacks.claim: Stripe subscription handling at purge is undefined. The purge cancels subscriptions after detaching payment methods and redacting metadata, with no stated ordering or failure handling. Unused paid time and refunds at purge are left to a policy the plan does not change.
attacks.evidence: "At purge, any still-active subscription is cancelled. Refunds follow the existing refund policy, linked from screen 1; nothing changes there." / "Stripe: detach payment methods and redact customer metadata"

attacks.claim: The user is never told the outcome. Completion and failure appear only on an internal dashboard, so Art. 12(3) information on the action taken is not delivered to the data subject.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no post-purge notice to the user. "A dashboard shows pending, completed and failed per processor."

attacks.claim: The confirmation email is the only notice of the 14-day window, but send failures are not monitored or retried, and the plan has no fallback. A user can lose the cancel window without knowing a deletion was requested.
attacks.evidence: "Your Parlo account will be deleted on {date}. Changed your mind? Log in before then, or use this link."

attacks.claim: Failures in the nightly AccountPurgeJob database step have no alert or ticket path. Only processor failures open tickets, so a failing transaction could silently miss the one-month deadline.
attacks.evidence: "anything still failing opens a `purge-failed` ticket for the privacy lead" applies only to processor calls. ABSENT: failure handling and alerting for the nightly DB transaction.

attacks.claim: The logged-out web flow says clicking the emailed link counts as re-auth, and the steps after that click are not specified. The plan does not say a final explicit confirm is required, so link prefetching by mail scanners or a forwarded link could trigger deletion without a deliberate user action.
attacks.evidence: "we email a confirmation link to the account address, and clicking it counts as re-auth." / ABSENT: the steps after the click.

attacks.claim: Anyone with access to the account inbox can trigger deletion via the email re-auth and can also cancel it, since the same inbox is the only factor. The 3/day rate limit is keyed on the address and does not limit this.
attacks.evidence: "The confirmation email gives the real owner 14 days to cancel even if their password was used."

attacks.claim: The single-use cancel link is valid until purge and does not require re-auth. Anyone who obtains the email can cancel a pending deletion.
attacks.evidence: "The link is single-use, signed, valid until the purge."

attacks.claim: The restore cutoff is ambiguous (nightly job versus displayed date), and a Keep-my-account request racing the purge is not described as atomic.
attacks.evidence: "restores the account exactly as it was" / "Logging in during the 14 days shows"

attacks.claim: deleted_accounts keeps purged user IDs and dates, which are still linkable pseudonymous data, so 'no PII' is doubtful. No retention period is given.
attacks.evidence: "Table `deleted_accounts` keeps only purged user IDs and dates (no PII)"

attacks.claim: The plan does not describe age-specific handling for the 16+ sign-up rule in deletion or export, including identity checks on the export email.
attacks.evidence: "Download my data first" links to the existing data export (emailed ZIP).

attacks.claim: No localisation plan is given for deletion copy or emails for EU users, so intelligibility in each user's language is unspecified.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: any mention of languages, translations or locale for Screen 1, Screen 3 or the emails.

attacks.claim: The 10-minute re-auth expiry gives no warning before it lapses, which can cost users on slow assistive tech their place.
attacks.evidence: "Re-auth is valid for 10 minutes; if it expires the user re-auths and returns to the same step"

attacks.claim: Screen 1 says club messages are permanently deleted, but rows owned by others are nullified, so users may misread what is removed.
attacks.evidence: "club messages and leaderboard history are permanently deleted 14 days after you confirm"

attacks.claim: Processor retries for up to 7 days across five processors have no throttle or rate-limit handling, and no batching is described for the nightly purge.
attacks.evidence: "Each call retries with exponential backoff for up to 7 days"

attacks.claim: The three-week schedule for two engineers covers many components with no buffer and no stated cut list if time runs short.
attacks.evidence: "Owners: 2 engineers (1 backend, 1 web/mobile) · 3 weeks · Epic PAR-2207"

attacks.claim: Staff accounts are the first deletion cohort, but no rule prevents a tester from deleting their own staff account during testing.
attacks.evidence: "Week 3: staff accounts (60) first, then 100%, then App Store resubmission the same week."
